question: Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument on Earth. Five stone towers rise above the Cambodian jungle. The Khmer arranged them to model one sacred mountain. Hindu myth calls that peak the home of the gods and the center of the universe. Which sacred mountain do the towers picture?
context: Mount Meru is the golden world-mountain at the heart of Hindu and Buddhist cosmology, imagined as the axis of the universe ringed by seas and continents. Angkor Wat's five towers rise in a quincunx -- four around one taller central peak -- turning the whole temple into a stone model of the cosmos with Meru at its center. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Wat (five towers in quincunx modelling Mount Meru); worldhistory.org/Angkor_Wat.  (Legend.)

question: At Cape Denison the wind almost never rests. Freezing, dense air pools on the high inland ice sheet, then slides seaward under its own weight, funnelling and accelerating as it drops toward the coast. Meteorologists have a special name for this kind of cold wind pouring off the ice. What is it called?
context: The word comes from the Greek katabatikos, 'going down.' Cold air is heavy, so where it collects on a high ice plateau it acts like an invisible flood -- spilling downhill under gravity and gathering speed, funnelled faster as the land narrows toward the coast. Chinook winds also blow downslope but WARM as they fall; trade winds and monsoons are driven by heat and the planet's rotation, not by cold air draining off ice. Antarctica's katabatic winds are the fiercest on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Bay

question: Lima sits right on the Pacific yet almost never sees rain. The reason runs in the water: a cold current sweeps north up the Peruvian coast, dragging deep water up so chilled that the sea here drops to about 16 C -- freezing for the tropics. That cold air can't rise to form rain clouds, so the coast stays a desert. What is this cold current called?
context: The cold Humboldt (Peru) Current, named for the German naturalist Alexander von Humboldt, drags deep water north up the coast, chilling the sea to about 16 C. Cold air can't rise to form rain clouds, which is the very reason the Peruvian coast is a desert despite fronting the ocean. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humboldt_Current.

question: Down the middle of the Atlantic runs the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a seam where fresh seafloor wells up and shoves Europe and North America apart by about 2.5 centimeters every year. That yearly creep almost exactly matches the growth rate of one part of your own body. Which?
context: Two and a half centimeters a year sounds like nothing, but over millions of years it pried open an entire ocean -- and it is still going, so the Atlantic is a little wider today than when you were born. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Atlantic_Ridge (corroborated by Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, https://www.whoi.edu/oceanus/feature/mid-atlantic-ridge-volcanic-processes/).

question: When the Salar de Uyuni dries out, its hard salt crust splits into a huge tiled floor of thousands of repeating shapes. Each shape is a meter or two across, and they fit edge to edge all the way to the horizon. What shape are these repeating salt tiles?
context: As the crust dries it cracks into a honeycomb of polygons a metre or two wide, tiling to the horizon. A 2023 study by Lasser and Goehring showed the hexagons form as salty water sinks and fresher water rises in convection 'rolls' below the crust, piling salt into ridges where neighbouring rolls meet. Source: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2023/03/230301101524.htm

question: In eastern Africa, a giant crack in the Earth's crust runs from the Red Sea down through Ethiopia, Kenya, and Tanzania. It is called the East African Rift, and it is a place where the continent is slowly tearing itself in two. Its two halves creep apart at only 8 to 9 millimetres a year. To picture that slow crawl, geologists like to compare it to the growth rate of one everyday thing on your own body. Which?
context: At roughly fingernail speed, the plates drift apart so gradually that the rift has taken over 20 million years to open this far. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Rift

question: In the maze of tidal channels where the Ganges delta meets the sea, one vast forest of salt-tolerant trees stands rooted in the brackish mud on tangled stilt-like roots, flooding and draining with every tide. It is the largest forest of its kind on the planet, shared between Bangladesh and India. What is this great tidal forest called?
context: The Sundarbans is the largest mangrove forest on Earth — about 10,277 sq km of tidal waterways, roughly 60% in Bangladesh and 40% in India (West Bengal), and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its name comes from the sundari mangrove tree. Source: Wikipedia 'Sundarbans'.

question: Stand on the San Andreas Fault and you feel nothing, yet two huge plates slide past each other all the time. They creep only about 20 to 35 mm a year. Geologists like to compare that slow speed to one thing on your body that grows just as slowly. What is it?
context: About 20-35 mm a year — a couple of centimetres, the pace a fingernail grows — is how fast California's greatest fault moves. It feels like nothing, yet kept up over millions of years it carries whole regions of the state northwest. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andreas_Fault.
